problem.plain: recognizing the same person across devices

format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo to CMO — on cross-device identity

Recommendation: stop trying to build one ID that works everywhere. It doesn't exist, and chasing it has cost the industry a decade.

Instead, I'd make identity a scored judgment, not a yes/no. Every link between two records gets a confidence number and a record of what consent permits. Then we set different bars per use case: suppression of existing customers can run on loose matches, because being wrong is cheap. Personalization and anything touching sensitive data needs a high bar.

First we need ground truth — a panel of people who tell us all their devices — so we can finally measure how wrong our matching actually is.

Expect this to shrink reported reach. That number was fiction; I'd rather know.
answers.first_move: Recruit a few thousand people who'll tell us every device they use, so we have a truth set to measure our matching against.
answers.hardest_part: Consent and identity change over time and across jurisdictions, so a link that was accurate and lawful on Tuesday may be neither by Friday, and nothing in the stack is built to expire gracefully.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: Chief Marketing Officer
Subject: A practical attack on cross-channel identity

I would not pursue a universal person ID; the incentives, laws and platform rules make that unlikely to be dependable. I would build a consent-bound identity layer with narrower promises. Start with authenticated, deterministic links—such as CRM login to app or commerce account—and record the purpose, source, jurisdiction and expiry of every link. Propagate revocation quickly and let channels operate independently when consent or evidence is missing.

Use probabilistic matching only for aggregated measurement, never for suppression or individual personalization where a false match could create privacy harm. Test the system against known identities to quantify false joins, missed links and bias by channel. Clean rooms can extend specific partnerships, not solve coverage. Success should mean less waste within measurable, consented segments—not recognition everywhere.
answers.first_move: Map every current identifier, consent signal and activation use to see where we have defensible links today.
answers.hardest_part: The genuinely hard part is preserving a person’s consent and revocation choices as identities, partners, laws and platform permissions change.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: Vendors keep selling universal fixes for recognizing customers across screens, but chasing an all-in-one identity graph is a money pit. The tech giants actively break cross-site tracking, and privacy laws will keep tightening. I would stop trying to stitch anonymous web visits together with probabilistic guesses; the error rate quietly ruins frequency caps and wastes spend. Instead, I would accept a smaller, honest footprint. We should focus entirely on giving people clear value to log in across our digital and store channels, and map only those authenticated moments under explicit consent. For everything else, we should rely on channel-level modeling rather than pretending we know the individual. It leaves blind spots, but it avoids legal landmines and fake certainty.
answers.first_move: Audit where we actually have confirmed, logged-in customer relationships versus where we are paying vendors to guess.
answers.hardest_part: The platforms controlling the devices make more money keeping their walls up than letting outsiders track people across them.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach: Move 1: Stop trying to build one identity graph and instead specify, per decision — suppression, frequency cap, personalization, measurement — the precision and recall each one actually needs, because suppressing a customer wrongly is a different kind of failure than capping a frequency wrongly and they should not share a threshold. What makes this hard: nobody in the chain owns the decision end-to-end, so the DSP, the CDP and the retailer each optimize match rate as a vanity number and there is no forum where the error budget gets agreed. Move 2: Build a calibration spine — a standing authenticated panel plus held-out deterministic links deliberately withheld from the graph — so every probabilistic edge carries a measured, continuously re-estimated error rate rather than a vendor's confidence score. What makes this hard: ground truth is itself consented, biased toward logged-in heavy users, and decays as device and household composition changes, so your calibration set is least representative exactly where matching is weakest. Move 3: Attach consent to the edge rather than the person — each link carries the purpose, jurisdiction and expiry under which it may be traversed, and the graph is resolved at decision time by walking only edges legal for that purpose, which means the same person resolves to different graphs for suppression versus personalization. What makes this hard: no current infrastructure passes purpose context down to the resolution layer, the signal is lost at the first hop, and edge-level evaluation is computationally far more expensive than a precomputed ID lookup at bid-stream latency. Where I disagree with the obvious answer: the industry keeps treating this as an identifier problem that a better ID (UID2, ID5, a clean room) will solve, but the ID is not the unit of value — the decision is, and a 70%-coverage graph with known error rates is operationally worth more than a 95%-coverage graph with unknown ones.
answers.first_move: Write down, for each marketing decision we make, how costly a wrong match is versus a missed one.
answers.hardest_part: There is no unbiased ground truth for cross-device identity, so error rates can only be estimated on the authenticated population where matching is already easiest.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
Move 1: Define a consent and purpose state machine before an identity graph, so every link is scoped by channel, use case, jurisdiction, provenance, and revocation rules.
What makes that move hard: Consent semantics differ across parties and laws, while revocation must propagate faster and more reliably than identity data.
Move 2: Build an opted-in deterministic benchmark across representative channels, then measure false links, missed links, bias, and decay for each matching method while allowing abstention.
What makes that move hard: Ground truth is scarce and systematically unrepresentative, so even rigorous validation may not predict performance for the users and environments that matter most.
Move 3: Pilot a federated, purpose-limited system that exchanges scoped tokens and calibrated match confidence rather than creating a universal person ID, starting with suppression and frequency control instead of personalization.
What makes that move hard: The design needs broad ecosystem participation, enforceable governance, and safeguards against correlated errors turning uncertain matches into durable privacy failures.
answers.first_move: Define the consent rules before building the identity graph.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is validating identity links without creating the invasive universal identity layer the system is meant to avoid.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: Move 1: Stop trying to build a universal identifier graph and instead anchor resolution to consumer-held cryptographic tokens that resolve locally on the device. What makes this hard is that everyday consumers have zero interest in managing identity keys unless every brand provides a massive, immediate economic payoff. Move 2: Treat cross-channel recognition as an ephemeral, transaction-scoped exchange negotiated in real time between endpoints rather than a stored profile. What makes this hard is that browser and operating system gatekeepers treat any coordinated cross-site state exchange as an exploit and will actively patch it out. Move 3: Cap individual resolution at verified first-party boundaries and force all cross-domain suppression and capping into differential-privacy cohort checks. What makes this hard is that ad buyers refuse to allocate budget to mechanisms that cannot be audited and reconciled row by row in a spreadsheet.
answers.first_move: Anchor resolution to consumer-held cryptographic tokens on the device instead of maintaining a backend identity graph.
answers.hardest_part: Platform gatekeepers will treat any workable protocol that coordinates state across separate domains as a fingerprinting vulnerability and intentionally break it.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```python
# 0. Premise: no universal ID is coming. Stop optimizing coverage; optimize *known* error.
#    The industry's real failure isn't match rate, it's that nobody can state their precision.

truth = consented_panel(multi_device, paid, refreshed_quarterly)   # your only ground truth.
# expect pain: panelists over-index on logged-in behavior, so measured precision is optimistic.
# correct for it or at least report the bias; don't pretend the panel is the population.

def resolve(signals, purpose):
    edges = deterministic(signals) + probabilistic(signals)        # one probability scale, no "tiers".
    for e in edges:                                                # a hashed-email match is just p=0.98, not a caste.
        e.p   = calibrate(e.score, truth, segment=(e.channel_a, e.channel_b))
                                                                   # calibrate per channel PAIR. web<->CTV and
                                                                   # web<->CRM have nothing in common; one global
                                                                   # threshold is where most graphs quietly fail.
        e.ok  = purpose in (consent(e.a) & consent(e.b))           # consent is a property of the EDGE, not the profile.
                                                                   # intersection, re-evaluated at query time, not merge time.
    return cluster(edges where e.ok, threshold=budget[purpose])    # resolve at read, per purpose. One canonical
                                                                   # person-graph is the original sin: it forces one
                                                                   # error rate onto uses with opposite cost functions.

budget = {
  "suppression":     0.95,   # false merge = suppress a real prospect; errors are invisible and compounding. be strict.
  "personalization": 0.92,   # false merge = creepy or wrong. strict.
  "frequency_cap":   0.60,   # over/under-merge both just waste money, roughly symmetrically. go loose.
  "measurement":     None,   # don't cluster at all. model p(link) into the estimator and deconvolve the bias.
}

# Disagreement with the obvious answer: frequency capping is a counting problem, not an identity problem.
# Push counters to the device/CTV app/publisher, cap locally, return sketches. You get global caps without
# ever resolving a person. This removes ~the largest single use case from the identity problem entirely.

emit(cluster, precision_recall_by_channel_pair, panel_vintage)    # ship the error bar with the ID or it's the status quo.
```
answers.first_move: Stand up a small paid consented multi-device panel and use it to measure the true precision of the matches we already make, per channel pair.
answers.hardest_part: Ground truth for cross-device linkage is itself identity data, so any panel large and clean enough to validate the graph is biased toward the logged-in people you didn't need help identifying.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Six items. The thing I'd push back on first: the obvious move is to pick an ID (UID2, ID5, LiveRamp, whatever) and declare it the spine. That's a procurement decision dressed up as an architecture decision, and it fails because you still can't say what your match error rate is. Precision is the unsolved part, not coverage. Second disagreement: cross-channel frequency capping probably does not need person-level resolution at all, and chasing it there is where most budget dies. Treat it as a measurement/allocation problem solved with panel calibration, and spend your identity budget on suppression and personalization, where the cost of being wrong is asymmetric and actually worth paying for.

1. Build a ground-truth set and publish your actual precision/recall. Take authenticated users who have logged in on 3+ surfaces (web, app, and one of CTV/retail/POS) in the last 90 days. Hold out 20% of those known links. Run your current resolution (vendor graph, internal graph, both) and report precision and recall against the holdout, segmented by channel pair and by whether the link came from deterministic, hashed-email, IP/household, or behavioral signal. DONE = a one-page table with numbers in it, circulated. Expect the CTV and offline cells to be embarrassing — household-level IP matching probably sits somewhere between 55% and 80% precision and nobody in the building currently knows which.

2. Set per-use-case confidence thresholds before you set any technology. Write down, for each of: opt-out suppression, do-not-contact/legal suppression, personalization, frequency capping, measurement — what false-positive rate is tolerable. Legal suppression tolerates almost no false negatives and lots of false positives (over-suppress, who cares). Personalization is the reverse: showing the wrong person's cart is a visible failure. DONE = a signed table of thresholds, and your resolution service returns a confidence score that gets compared against them at call time rather than returning a boolean.

3. Make consent a traveling record, not a flag on a profile. Model it as (subject, purpose, jurisdiction, lawful basis, source, timestamp, expiry) and require that every resolution join carries the most restrictive consent across the merged identities. DONE = you can answer, for any single activation, which consent record authorized it and which jurisdiction's rules were applied, from a log, without asking a human. The subtle failure here is consent laundering through the graph: linking a consented ID to a non-consented one and inheriting permission upward. Write the test that catches it.

4. Instrument decay. Pick a cohort of links, re-verify them monthly against fresh authenticated events, and produce a half-life curve by link type. DONE = you can state how long a hashed-email link, an IP-household link, and a MAID link stay valid. This is the number that determines whether you refresh weekly or quarterly, and it's the number vendors will not give you.

5. Use the clean room for calibration, not activation. Run one match-rate-and-overlap study with your largest retail media or platform partner whose only output is: how much of our audience do they see, and how does our internal graph's precision compare to theirs on the shared subset. DONE = a calibration factor you apply to planning numbers. Do not architect activation around a clean room this quarter; the cost-per-query economics and the inability to move individual decisions out make it a measurement instrument, not a spine.

6. Ship one channel pair end-to-end, instrumented, instead of a platform. Pick the pair with the highest business value and the best ground truth — usually CRM-to-web or CRM-to-retail-media. Run it with thresholds from item 2 and consent from item 3. DONE = a live campaign where you can report incremental reach, suppression accuracy, and the consent basis for every decision. The honest expectation is that you cover 30-50% of your addressable base well and the rest stays contextual or household-level, and the useful output of the quarter is knowing precisely which 30-50%.

What I'd expect to go wrong: the ground-truth set in item 1 is biased toward heavy multi-device users, so your measured precision will be optimistic for exactly the light-engagement population you most want to resolve. I don't have a clean fix for that beyond weighting and saying so out loud. Also expect that once you publish real precision numbers, someone senior will prefer the vendor's unverified match rate, because it's bigger.
answers.first_move: Pull the users who've logged in on three or more surfaces, hide some of those known connections, and see whether our current matching finds them back.
answers.hardest_part: You can only measure match accuracy on people who are already easy to match, so the error rate on the population you actually care about stays fundamentally unobservable.

answers.first_move: I would first narrow the work to specific permitted use cases instead of trying to build a universal identity graph.
answers.hardest_part: The genuinely hard part is that consent, identity confidence and platform permission all change independently, while mistakes can either expose data or suppress the wrong person.

answers.hardest_part: Platform walled gardens and privacy laws deliberately reward isolation, making the open web's technical incentives work against reliable, real-time unlinking when consent changes.

format.label: Fifty words
format.instruction: Fifty words or fewer. No preamble, no caveats. The compression is the point: keep only what you would keep if you could keep one thing.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach: Stop chasing one ID. Treat identity as a probability distribution with calibrated confidence, consent attached per edge, and different thresholds per use case — suppression tolerates error, personalization doesn't. Measure link accuracy against held-out deterministic truth, publish error rates. Expect the ground truth itself to be biased toward logged-in people.
answers.first_move: Pick one use case and ask what match error rate it can actually tolerate.
answers.hardest_part: You can only validate matches against logged-in users, who are exactly the population least representative of the ones you're guessing about.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Hush now, the graph that we built in the spring
is mostly just email and hope on a string —
so stop chasing one ID to rule them all,
and measure the error instead of the sprawl.

I'd start with a truth set, small, panel-born, true,
to score every link as a probability too;
then spend that uncertainty channel by channel —
loose for frequency, tight for the suppression panel.

Consent rides along as a field, not a gate,
versioned and dated, revocable, straight;
if a link can't say why it's allowed to exist,
it falls off the graph and it won't be missed.

The clean rooms stay blind to the people they lack,
and CTV still won't hand the household back —
so sleep, little marketer, nothing is solved;
we just know our error, and that's how we evolved.
answers.first_move: Build a small panel of people whose real cross-device behavior we know, so we can finally measure how often our matches are wrong.
answers.hardest_part: Nobody can see the ground truth of who a person actually is across walled gardens, so every match rate we report is a guess measuring itself.
